1.0.s.en: (1) The places where the commandments were given

1.0.0.en: Beyond the Jordan: the eastern bank of the Jordan River.

1.0.2.en: The plain (Arabah): the valley (plain) extending from the southern end of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Suph: what is meant here is the Gulf of Aqaba; the name Sea of Suph is applied to the whole Red Sea, or to the gulf as part of the sea.

1.0.3.en: Paran: the name of the desert extending through the eastern region of the Sinai Peninsula, parallel to the line running from El-Arish to Eilat (anciently Ezion-geber). Tophel: a place about 20 km south-east of the Dead Sea; it may be the present village of Tafileh, which has 600 inhabitants.

1.0.4.en: Laban: or Libnah, which lies a few kilometres north-east of Hazeroth.

1.0.5.en: Hazeroth: about 40 km north-east of Mount Horeb; it is where Miriam, the sister of Moses, became leprous (Num 12) (maps 1, 12).

1.0.6.en: Dizahab: on the line of march from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea, among the mountains, between the wilderness of Paran to the west and the Gulf of Aqaba to the east. Its meaning is "the place where there is much gold."

1.0.7.en: These are the commandments of Moses to his people before his departure from this world, and they are for the people of God in every generation.

1.0.8.en: Moses specified the place where he met with the people and spoke to them in three sermons (and to simplify matters for the reader we say that this place is east of the Jordan River). Here begins the first of these sermons, which is recorded in (ch. 1-5). He probably spoke to the elders of Israel and not to the whole people, whose number exceeded 2 million persons, and the seventy elders conveyed his words to all the people.

1.0.9.en: We shall notice in this sermon, although it is the farewell address of Moses, who had reached the age of 120 years and whose life was drawing to its end, that he did not speak of his own achievements and his labor with his people, but spoke of God's love and care for them, so that the people would remember this and not be distracted from God by the good things of the Promised Land into which they were about to enter. Moses also did not speak of the wars they would fight to possess the Promised Land, but spoke of God's care for them; for what matters is their relationship with God, and by His power victory in all wars will be easy for them.

1.1.0.en: Eleven days: a traveler on foot walks about 8 hours a day, covering 20 miles in them, or 15 miles if they are a caravan. The distance between Horeb and Kadesh-barnea is 165 miles, so it takes 11 days.

1.1.1.en: Horeb: the region around Mount Sinai, on which Moses received the Ten Commandments.

1.1.2.en: Mount Seir: south of the Dead Sea.

1.1.3.en: Kadesh-barnea: in the middle of the line extending from El-Arish to the head of the Gulf of Aqaba.

1.1.4.en: The journey between Horeb and Kadesh-barnea takes 11 days, but the journey of the children of Israel in Sinai took 40 years. This was because of the hardness of their hearts and their refusal to obey God by entering the Promised Land and rooting out the wicked, so God made them wander in the wilderness until the stubborn generation died and their sons entered the Promised Land.

1.1.5.en: It is to be noted that the Book of Deuteronomy consists of teachings from Moses to the new people after the death of all the fathers, except Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh. In this it differs from the books of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers, in which we hear of God's conversations with Moses. Here he strengthens the people in faith in God and in holding fast to His commandments and laws, so that they would not be alarmed by the might of the enemies in the land of Canaan, nor forget His laws amid the pagan worship prevalent in Canaan.

1.1.6.en: Be obedient to God's commandments however difficult they may seem, for they are the shortest way to enter the Kingdom, and be confident that God will support you and deliver you from every evil if you obey His commandments.

1.2.s.en: (2) Remembering the defeat of Sihon and Og

1.2.0.en: The addresses of Moses to his people took place at the end of the fortieth year after the children of Israel left Egypt. He repeated to them the rulings of the divine Law which he had transmitted to them, and followed them with his counsel that they should not turn aside from it and his warning to them of what would befall them if they transgressed it. The timing of these addresses was a short time before his repose and the handing over of leadership to Joshua.

1.2.1.en: Moses began his address on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year, and the people crossed the Jordan River and entered the Promised Land on the tenth day of the first month of the forty-first year (Josh 4:19). The whole period is therefore sixty-nine days. Moses spent about thirty days in the addresses recorded in the Book of Deuteronomy, and they mourned for him thirty days (ch. 34:8), and in the few remaining days the Law was written and handed over to the Levites.

1.3.0.en: The Amorites: a Semitic people of Canaanite origin. In the time of Moses they lived in the south of Palestine, and at some period of their history they also ruled the region east of the Jordan, from the Arnon River in the south to Mount Hermon in the north.

1.3.1.en: Heshbon: the city of Sihon king of the Amorites in the time of Moses. In its place today is a ruined city known as "Hesban," between the Arnon River and the Jabbok River.

1.3.2.en: Bashan: a province in the land of Canaan lying east of the Jordan between Mount Hermon and Mount Gilead, bounded on the north by Damascus, on the east by the Syrian desert, on the south by the land of Gilead and on the west by the Jordan River, and crossed in the east by the Druze Mountain (map 5). Astaroth: a town in Bashan that was the capital of Og king of Bashan; it is thought to be the present Tell Ashtara, 35 km east of the Sea of Galilee.

1.3.3.en: Edrei: the capital of Bashan, whose present name is "Daraa"; it lies about 47 km east of the southern end of the Sea of Galilee, on the border between Jordan and Syria.

1.3.4.en: Beyond the Jordan: the eastern bank of the Jordan (maps 4, 13). The people, under the leadership of Moses, reached this spot, which lies on the eastern bank of the Jordan in the land of Moab, after two wars in which Israel defeated both Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. Sihon controlled the southern part east of the Jordan River while Og ruled its northern part. The news of this victory is given in the Book of Numbers (ch. 21) (map 5).

1.4.0.en: The land of Moab: the eastern part of the Dead Sea region, which is today part of the Kingdom of Jordan. Moses was not content to repeat the Law, but also explained and interpreted it for the new generation, which was about to enter the land of Canaan after the previous generation had perished entirely in the wilderness.

1.4.1.en: It is good to remember God's former works with you, so that you may be reassured, give thanks and take courage in your striving, relying on His power.

1.5.s.en: (3) God's call to enter the land of Canaan

1.5.0.en: The children of Israel reached Mount Horeb on the first day of the third month in the first year of their departure from Egypt, and they remained there about a year, during which they received the commandments and the Law and made the Tabernacle of Meeting as God had commanded them. But afterwards they refused to enter the Promised Land, so He made them wander in the wilderness of Sinai for 40 years.

1.6.0.en: The mount of the Amorites: it is in the south of Palestine, and the Amorites had five kings in it (Josh 10:5). The Arabah: the great rift in which the Jordan River flows.

1.6.1.en: The mountains, the plain and the south: the plain is the low-lying lands adjoining the Mediterranean Sea and extending from the north of Palestine to its south; the mountains are the central highlands; and the south is the Negev region extending from the south of Palestine to the border of Egypt.

1.6.2.en: The seaside: the coastal regions on the Mediterranean Sea.

1.6.3.en: The land of Canaan: what is meant by it is all the land of Palestine and its surroundings, inhabited by the Canaanite peoples. Lebanon to the great river, the river Euphrates: what is meant is present-day Lebanon, which extends along the Mediterranean coast, and then the lands extending east of it as far as the Euphrates River.

1.6.4.en: The Lord asked them to journey and enter the mount of the Amorites in the south of Palestine and head north to the great river, that is, the Euphrates River; this is the land promised to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, for the Lord longed to hasten to fulfill His promise to give them possession of the land.

1.6.5.en: Unbelief in God's promises makes us stray from His commandments, so that we wander in this world and are exposed to being lost in sins and scattered in worldly thoughts that take us away from the way of life which God has drawn for us, as He said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life," and thus we walk in labyrinths that take us away from the Kingdom which the Lord promised to those who obey His commandments.

1.7.s.en: (4) The appointment of elders to help Moses

1.7.0.en: Before continuing the events of the main story, whose beginning is mentioned in (vv. 6-8) and which tells what happened when the Lord asked them to enter the Promised Land and possess it, Moses turns to another event that also took place at Horeb, the appointment of a number of judges to decide the cases of the people (Ex 18:13-27); for it was very difficult for Moses alone to judge and resolve the problems of 2 million souls.

1.8.0.en: As He has spoken to you: He promised your fathers.

1.8.1.en: The number of the people increased greatly, as God had promised Abraham, and consequently the problems that inevitably arise among individuals and groups so numerous also increased; this is natural with the growth in numbers. Moses blesses them and asks God to increase their numbers more and more.

1.9.0.en: Moses decided to take the counsel of his father-in-law (Jethro) (the story recorded in Ex 18:13-27), so he appointed a number of wise men to help him in deciding disputes, and the people welcomed this.

1.10.0.en: Known men (heads): persons who knew the word of God so as to judge by it among their brethren. They were probably like counselors who judged for all the tribes, that is, for the people in general and not for a particular group, and they were distinguished in understanding and knowledge. Many of them may have been among the foremen who led the people of Israel in Egypt to gather bricks and build the cities which the Egyptians forced them to build (Ex 5:6).

1.10.1.en: Hear: give attention to hearing the complaints and problems of the people, so that you may judge and resolve them for them.

1.10.2.en: Moses divided the people into small groups, that is, tens, and appointed a judge over each; then over every few groups he appointed a higher judge, and so on until he appointed a judge ruling over thousands of them. He also appointed general counselors whom he called heads, and gave them much advice for this work of theirs, and commanded them to hold fast to the truth in their judgments, without any ulterior purpose, whether between the Jews and one another or between them and the strangers dwelling among them. It is to be noted that God did not choose them from the rich or those of high position, but chose them for their wisdom, discernment, understanding and care for His word, so that they might teach the people by it.

1.11.0.en: For the judgment is God's: you are judges on God's behalf, to judge by His word, so you must be just as He is.

1.11.1.en: These instructions were not to show partiality in judgment and not to fear any man in their judging, however high his standing, and to bring to him every matter too hard for them to judge.

1.11.2.en: Let us not despise the counsels offered to us by others, even if they are of lower standing than we are, just as Moses the leader accepted the counsel of his pagan father-in-law; nor let us scorn them, but accept what is good in them in a spirit of humility, so that we benefit from the counsel of others.

1.12.s.en: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

1.12.0.en: The great and terrible wilderness: the northern regions of the wilderness of Sinai, which are rugged and wide, and passing through them is dangerous because they are barren and have wild beasts, in addition to the wicked peoples living in and around it; but God by His care preserved them in it.

1.12.1.en: The mount of the Amorites: one of the most important landmarks of the way in this wilderness, which we have mentioned in (v. 7) (map 1). Moses resumes the main story in this chapter, so the present verses can be read directly after (vv. 6-8) in order to follow the continuity of the story.

1.12.2.en: The people departed from Horeb as the Lord commanded and came to Kadesh-barnea (maps 1, 12).

1.13.0.en: Here Moses made them understand that by this they had reached the mount of the Amorites, which the Lord had promised them would be the first stage of the way to their possessing the land, and therefore it is the gateway leading to the rest of the promised land.

1.14.0.en: Moses reassures them that there is no need for fear or dread in facing the inhabitants of the land, because it is the Lord who commanded them to go up and possess the land.

1.15.0.en: The people did not carry out God's command immediately to go up and possess the land, but decided to send out a reconnaissance party to spy out the land before entering it as warriors. This may have been sound military thinking, practiced even in our present world, but the motive for sending the spies was their fear of the unknown in the new land, because of the weakness of their faith in God and their disobedience to Him. When they asked Moses to send spies, he spoke to God, and God agreed, not because this was the right course of action but because of His longsuffering toward the people (Num 13:1, 2). Sadly, when the spies returned, ten of them proclaimed the strength of the enemies and the impossibility of overcoming them, so the people were afraid and followed them, and rejected the encouragement of Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, the two spies who showed the blessing of God and His good things in the land and His power able to support the people. When the people murmured against God, He was angry with them and did not bring them into the Promised Land, but made them wander in the wilderness until all the murmurers died, and only their sons entered the Promised Land.

1.16.0.en: Therefore Moses agreed with them in this and sent the party, choosing one man from each tribe.

1.17.0.en: The valley of Eshcol: a valley near Hebron to the north, still famous today for its vineyards; it is the valley of Hebron or the valley of Mamre (map 2).

1.17.1.en: They went up to the mount of the Amorites and came to the valley of Eshcol. The Book of Numbers gave the details of the places through which the spies passed, and their journey took forty days (Num 13:21-25).

1.18.0.en: They took samples of the fruit of the land and its abundant good things, then returned to their tribes saying that the land was good and fruitful.

1.18.1.en: If you become troubled by anything, do not stir up those around you and do not yield to thoughts of doubt and tension, but turn to God in prayer and ask for the guidance of your father of confession, so that you may calm down and God may guide you to the right solution and you may guide those around you, so that you become a cause of blessing to others and not of disturbance.

1.19.s.en: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

1.19.0.en: Despite what the spies brought as confirmation of the truth of the Lord's promises that the land was good, "flowing with milk and honey," the weakness of the people's faith made them not trust the Lord's call to them to enter the land; on the contrary, they thought of appointing a leader for themselves other than Moses in order to return to Egypt (Num 14:1-4).

1.20.0.en: The sons of Anak: the descendants of Anak, a Canaanite man. They were described as giants because of their tall stature and the might of their strength in wars, and they are proverbial for their multitude and enormous size. They lived in the south of Palestine between Jerusalem and Hebron.

1.20.1.en: When they heard the spies say that the people of the land were very strong, that the cities were completely fortified against any foreign invasion and that the sons of Anak lived there, they were very afraid.

1.21.0.en: Moses reassured them, since he trusted in the Lord, and he had warned them before not to fear or be afraid of the inhabitants of the land.

1.22.0.en: Moses reminded them of all the works which the Lord had done with them and which they had witnessed with their own eyes since they were in Egypt, and that it was He who led them in the wilderness by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, and it was He who would bring them into the land of Canaan by His great power.

1.23.0.en: Moses also reminded them of God's care for them in the wilderness of Sinai, and how He fed them with manna and gave them drink from the rock and preserved their clothes and their sandals, and they passed safely on the way until He brought them to the threshold of the Promised Land. He likened God's care for them to a man who carries his child in his arms and looks after all his needs, so that he lacks nothing.

1.24.0.en: Moses rebuked them for their lack of faith in God's power which had led them in the wilderness of Sinai by the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, and how He chose for them suitable places to settle. Now He has prepared for them the land of Canaan, filled with good things, and by His power He is able to bring them into it; so why are they afraid?!

1.24.1.en: It may appear to us during our journey in life that the way of the Kingdom is a hard way, for it is a way of continual warfare against the enemy of good, which requires of us spiritual striving and constant vigilance, so we fear and shrink from walking in this hard way and forget that God is our defender and that the wars are the Lord's wars. Let us have complete confidence in God's victory over the world, as the Lord Christ assured us, saying, "Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."

1.25.s.en: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

1.25.0.en: The people's conduct in this situation brought upon them the wrath of the Lord, so He inflicted the punishment fitting for this disobedience.

1.26.0.en: When God saw the people's murmuring and their attempt to return to Egypt, He declared that all of them were deprived of entering the Promised Land, except the two who believed in Him and encouraged the people. One of them is mentioned here, Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who would possess the land on which he had trodden, that is, he would take his portion of the land of Canaan. In this verse He did not mention "Joshua," his companion, but will mention him in (v. 38), because he would not only enter the Promised Land but would lead the whole people as successor to Moses.

1.27.0.en: For your sakes: because of your frequent murmuring, I was driven to strike the rock twice and sinned against God.

1.27.1.en: In humility, Moses shows his weakness in striking the rock twice at Meribah (Num 20:10-12), contrary to God's command; for he was strained by the repeated murmurings of the children of Israel and struck the rock twice instead of once. Therefore God deprived him of entering the Promised Land because of the weakness of his faith. But this did not diminish the greatness of Moses, whom the Church considers the chief of the prophets and who is the greatest figure in the eyes of the Jews. All this confirms the gravity of the murmuring into which the children of Israel fell and of their disobedience to God.

1.28.0.en: Who stands before you: your disciple who assists you.

1.28.1.en: Encourage him: Moses laid his hands on Joshua, encouraged him and gave him counsels, and did all this before the people as a declaration that he was his successor, so that they would respect him and submit to him (Num 27:20, 22, 23; Deut 31:7, 8). God commanded Moses to strengthen Joshua and declare before the people that he was his successor, to lead the children of Israel after him and bring them into the Promised Land.

1.29.0.en: God will fulfill His promise in the next generation, those who were children at that time, that is, less than twenty years old, whom the fathers feared would fall into captivity or be killed in the battles with the sons of Anak. The Lord promises that these sons will inherit the Promised Land because they are innocent of the disobedience of their fathers, for their young age at that time did not allow them to know good and evil.

1.30.0.en: Since God was angry with the people, He kept them away from the Promised Land and turned them into the wilderness of Sinai toward the Red Sea, to wander in this wilderness for about 40 years, during which all the adults who murmured would die; then He would bring their sons back to the threshold of the Promised Land, where Moses is now speaking to them before his death and just before their entering the Promised Land.

1.30.1.en: Do not make light of God's longsuffering by murmuring against your life and refusing to carry out His commandments, for He is just and able to deprive you of many blessings which you enjoy now. If you fall into murmuring, return quickly to Him in repentance and thank Him for His gifts, because He is a tender Father who wants to forgive you all your sins.

1.31.s.en: (8) The defeat of Israel before the peoples of the land

1.31.0.en: The children of Israel realized their error toward God when He declared His wrath against them by depriving them of entering the Promised Land, but they did not repent; rather, they rushed to enter the Promised Land without praying and seeking God's help. They felt their strength after arming themselves, putting on belts and weapons of war, and made light of going up the mountain and attacking the enemies, trusting in their own strength and not in God.

1.32.0.en: When God saw their rushing to fight the enemies relying on their own strength, He had compassion on them in His fatherhood and warned them against entering the Promised Land, for this was not obedience to His commands but rashness and pride on their part. He warned them that He would not be with them and therefore they would be defeated before the enemies.

1.33.0.en: You were presumptuous: you were proud and insolent.

1.33.1.en: God reminded them that they had not obeyed Him, but in pride trusted in their own strength and rushed toward the mountains in the south of Palestine to go up them, fight the enemies and possess their land.

1.34.0.en: Hormah: on the border of Edom near Ziklag.

1.34.1.en: The land of Seir: a land that the Horites inhabited (Gen 14:6), then Esau and his descendants took possession of it (Gen 32:3); it was also called Mount Seir, and the land of Seir lies south of the Dead Sea (map 13). God reminded them that when they disobeyed Him and attacked the Amorites, the Amorites came out against them and drove them from their land, as bees drive away anyone who attacks their hives, and kept pursuing them as far as Hormah, a town on the border of the land of Edom in the south of Palestine. When the children of Israel returned in great sorrow after many of them had been killed, God did not listen to their cry because they had not repented.

1.35.0.en: The children of Israel stayed in Kadesh with hearts full of grief over their defeat before the enemies, for many days, which some think were forty days, like the period they spent in Kadesh waiting for the spies to return from their mission of spying out the Promised Land. After that they journeyed in the wilderness for about 38 years in wandering until all the murmuring people died, and then they returned again to Kadesh so that the sons might enter the Promised Land.

1.35.1.en: The enemy of good often makes us imagine that our earthly wisdom is better than divine counsel, so we make decisions and walk in ways that do not agree with what God has drawn for us, and after entering into temptation the error of our choices and the troubles they have caused us become clear to us. Let us always set God's will before our eyes and leave the leadership to Him to direct our life according to His good will.

1.35.2.en: The march of victory over Sihon king of the Amorites
